prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Compared to the adjacent cycle path, the cycle lane has stronger lane markings which increases the Ease of Use for cyclists. Additionally, it runs on the road level next to the motor traffic and is usually better asphalted than cycle paths. This allows a more fluent cycling and increases the Physical Comfort. Interestingly, the cycle lane is rated slightly more negatively on Mental Comfort than on Interaction. A well marked cycle lane is often considered as a proper cycling facility that draws drivers’ attention to possible cyclists. However, although it separates from the motor traffic and, therefore, leads to less possible interactions, cyclists might perceive it as mentally uncomfortable because of a small width and a lack of feeling safe. Generally spoken, the less the cycling facility is separated the worse it is rated on the clusters. Surprisingly, the bicycle boulevard is evaluated similar to the least separated advisory lane, but with a much better rating in Mental Comfort. This indicates that a too weak separation can no longer induce a feeling of safety or Mental Comfort, and below this threshold of separation, cyclists might prefer bicycle boulevards which draw attention to cyclists as road users, but in principle have no separation at all. More concrete, cyclists may prefer no separation over a too weak one. Bicycle boulevards are also evaluated more positively than residential roads, although in Germany, bicycle boulevards are usually open for motorized traffic and the traffic regulations are, hence, the same as for residential roads. The only difference are traffic signs that highlight cyclists as road users who must not be endangered by motor vehicles, and that cyclists are allowed to cycle side by side (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, 2020). On the one hand, this may lead to a stronger self-confidence of the cyclists towards other road users. Cyclists may feel uncomfortable here as they cycle on a way which is mainly for walking, and cycling is only tolerated. Cyclists are, thus, in the position of the stronger road user that must be considerate towards the weaker and slower pedestrians. Negative ratings in this cluster apply for traffic lights and cobbled stone, whereas asphalt, low traffic volume, the cycle lane, and the separated cycle path were rated positively. In contrast to Mental Comfort, it represents the physical aspect of the term comfort such as physical effort or the ability to cycle fluently without any obstacles. It also suits the concept of convenience in terms of the suitability and usefulness of a route to get fast and easy from A to B (Chen et al., 2018; Vallejo-Borda et al., 2020). It is interesting to see that this cluster contains the constructs where participants explicitly mentioned the term comfort. Whereas in the literature the concept of comfort is used either in a physical (Ayachi et al., 2015; Bíl et al., 2015) or in a cognitive way (Caviedes & Figliozzi, 2018), in this study, participants mentioned the term comfort almost exclusively in terms of physical comfort. Example constructs are “pleasant cycling vs. shaken about” or “Nice to cycle vs. feels bumpy”. When referring to comfort in terms of cognitively stress-free cycling, participants mentioned the terms stress-free or relaxed, but not the term comfortable. Accordingly, this cluster is rated positively at cycle facilities, asphalt, and low traffic volume, that is, in situations with smooth surface and without possible obstacles or crossing road users. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

That is, groups of similar constructs were created and labelled and further specified, extended, split, or merged in the course of categorization until all constructs were assigned in satisfactory categories. For this categorization, only the constructs’ names were used, not the ratings. To validate the categories, the assignment of the constructs to the categories was repeated separately by rater A and a third rater C. These assignments were then compared to the first assignment to calculate the intrarater and the interrater reliability, respectively. The intrarater reliability described by Cohen’s Kappa gave κ =0.895 which is an “almost perfect” (Landis & Koch, 1977, p.165) agreement. With regard to the interrater reliability, κ =0.802 indicates a “substantial” (Landis & Koch, 1977, p.165) agreement. The further analyses were based on the second assignment of rater A. The cycle lane is most positively rated on Physical Comfort and Ease of Use. Compared to the adjacent cycle path, the cycle lane has stronger lane markings which increases the Ease of Use for cyclists. Additionally, it runs on the road level next to the motor traffic and is usually better asphalted than cycle paths. This allows a more fluent cycling and increases the Physical Comfort. Interestingly, the cycle lane is rated slightly more negatively on Mental Comfort than on Interaction. A well marked cycle lane is often considered as a proper cycling facility that draws drivers’ attention to possible cyclists. However, although it separates from the motor traffic and, therefore, leads to less possible interactions, cyclists might perceive it as mentally uncomfortable because of a small width and a lack of feeling safe. Generally spoken, the less the cycling facility is separated the worse it is rated on the clusters. Surprisingly, the bicycle boulevard is evaluated similar to the least separated advisory lane, but with a much better rating in Mental Comfort. This indicates that a too weak separation can no longer induce a feeling of safety or Mental Comfort, and below this threshold of separation, cyclists might prefer bicycle boulevards which draw attention to cyclists as road users, but in principle have no separation at all. More concrete, cyclists may prefer no separation over a too weak one. Bicycle boulevards are also evaluated more positively than residential roads, although in Germany, bicycle boulevards are usually open for motorized traffic and the traffic regulations are, hence, the same as for residential roads. The only difference are traffic signs that highlight cyclists as road users who must not be endangered by motor vehicles, and that cyclists are allowed to cycle side by side (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, 2020). On the one hand, this may lead to a stronger self-confidence of the cyclists towards other road users. On the other hand, cyclists may associate a bicycle boulevard with even lower traffic volume, lower traffic speed, and more cooperative and careful interactions with other road users which increases their perception of Interaction, Environment, and Mental Comfort compared to the residential road. The shared footpath is evaluated neither good nor bad on all the clusters. The Mental and Physical Comfort are even lower than at bicycle boulevards and shared spaces. Cyclists may feel uncomfortable here as they cycle on a way which is mainly for walking, and cycling is only tolerated. Cyclists are, thus, in the position of the stronger road user that must be considerate towards the weaker and slower pedestrians. Also, cyclists need to watch out for people leaving buildings or properties and suddenly stepping onto the footpath. All this might be perceived as stressful and as hindering the cycling flow. The ratings of Ease of Use are less negative, that is, none of the elements is very poor on this criterion. The least positive rating applies to the shared space which makes sense as in this situation cyclists have to find their way together with motor vehicles and pedestrians. Again, the two cycle paths and the cycle lane as well as low traffic volume were rated positively. The cluster Physical Comfort includes the categories surface, comfort, and unhindered cycling. Negative ratings in this cluster apply for traffic lights and cobbled stone, whereas asphalt, low traffic volume, the cycle lane, and the separated cycle path were rated positively. In contrast to Mental Comfort, it represents the physical aspect of the term comfort such as physical effort or the ability to cycle fluently without any obstacles. It also suits the concept of convenience in terms of the suitability and usefulness of a route to get fast and easy from A to B (Chen et al., 2018; Vallejo-Borda et al., 2020). It is interesting to see that this cluster contains the constructs where participants explicitly mentioned the term comfort. Whereas in the literature the concept of comfort is used either in a physical (Ayachi et al., 2015; Bíl et al., 2015) or in a cognitive way (Caviedes & Figliozzi, 2018), in this study, participants mentioned the term comfort almost exclusively in terms of physical comfort. Example constructs are “pleasant cycling vs. shaken about” or “Nice to cycle vs. feels bumpy”. When referring to comfort in terms of cognitively stress-free cycling, participants mentioned the terms stress-free or relaxed, but not the term comfortable. Accordingly, this cluster is rated positively at cycle facilities, asphalt, and low traffic volume, that is, in situations with smooth surface and without possible obstacles or crossing road users. Negative ratings were found at the traffic light and cobbled stone, that is, in situation associated with physical effort in terms of high energy consumption due to starting after a stop (Fajans & Curry, 2001) or a high rolling resistance (Ho¨lzel et al., 2012). 4.3.
